name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_FLUIDS_NUMERICAL_Q01 - Mass of mercury filling a cylindrical container

questiontext.text: A laboratory flask of volume \(2.50 \times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m}^3\) is completely filled with mercury at standard temperature and pressure. Given that the density of mercury is \(13.6 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\), what is the mass of the mercury contained in the flask?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Volume of flask: \(V = 2.50 \times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m}^3\). Density of mercury: \(\rho = 13.6 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formula
Density is defined as mass per unit volume: \[\rho = \frac{m}{V} \implies m = \rho V.\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Multiply density by volume: \[m = (13.6 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}) \times (2.50 \times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m}^3) = 13.6 \times 0.250 = 3.40\,\mathrm{kg}.\]

Final Answer:
The mass of the mercury contained in the flask is \(3.40\,\mathrm{kg}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_FLUIDS_NUMERICAL_Q02 - Average pressure exerted by normal force on plate

questiontext.text: A compressive force of magnitude \(250\,\mathrm{N}\) acts perpendicularly on a flat metal plate of area \(0.050\,\mathrm{m}^2\). What is the average pressure exerted on the plate?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Normal force: \(F = 250\,\mathrm{N}\). Surface area: \(A = 0.050\,\mathrm{m}^2\).

Step 2: Relevant Formula
Average pressure is defined as normal force per unit area: \[P_{\mathrm{av}} = \frac{F}{A}.\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the given values: \[P_{\mathrm{av}} = \frac{250\,\mathrm{N}}{0.050\,\mathrm{m}^2} = 5000\,\mathrm{N}\,\mathrm{m}^{-2} = 5.0 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{Pa}.\]

Final Answer:
The average pressure exerted on the plate is \(5.0 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{Pa}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_FLUIDS_NUMERICAL_Q03 - Relative density of ethyl alcohol from absolute density

questiontext.text: The density of ethyl alcohol at standard temperature and pressure is \(0.806 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\). Taking the density of water at \(4^\circ\mathrm{C}\) as \(1.00 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\), what is the relative density of ethyl alcohol?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Density of ethyl alcohol: \(\rho_{\text{alcohol}} = 0.806 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\). Density of water at \(4^\circ\mathrm{C}\): \(\rho_{\text{water}} = 1.00 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formula
Relative density is a dimensionless scalar defined as the ratio of substance density to water density at \(4^\circ\mathrm{C}\): \[\text{Relative Density} = \frac{\rho_{\text{alcohol}}}{\rho_{\text{water}}}.\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Divide the densities: \[\text{Relative Density} = \frac{0.806 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}}{1.00 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}} = 0.806.\]

Final Answer:
The relative density of ethyl alcohol is \(0.806\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_FLUIDS_NUMERICAL_Q04 - Conversion of pressure from torr to atmospheres

questiontext.text: A pressure gauge indicates a pressure of \(1520\,\mathrm{torr}\). What is this pressure expressed in atmospheres (\(\mathrm{atm}\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Pressure value: \(P = 1520\,\mathrm{torr}\). Standard atmospheric pressure: \(1\,\mathrm{atm} = 760\,\mathrm{torr}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formula
The conversion from torr to atmospheres is: \[P (\mathrm{atm}) = \frac{P (\mathrm{torr})}{760\,\mathrm{torr}\,\mathrm{atm}^{-1}}.\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate the ratio: \[P = \frac{1520}{760} = 2.0\,\mathrm{atm}.\]

Final Answer:
The pressure is equal to \(2.0\,\mathrm{atm}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_FLUIDS_NUMERICAL_Q05 - Water column height equivalent to standard atmospheric pressure

questiontext.text: If water of density \(1.00 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\) is used in a barometer instead of mercury, what height of water column corresponds to an atmospheric pressure of \(1.00 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}\)? (Take \(g = 10\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Atmospheric pressure: \(P_a = 1.00 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}\). Density of water: \(\rho = 1.00 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\). Gravitational acceleration: \(g = 10\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formula
The barometric equation is: \[P_a = \rho g h \implies h = \frac{P_a}{\rho g}.\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the parameters: \[h = \frac{1.00 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}}{(1.00 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3})(10\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2})} = \frac{10^5}{10^4} = 10.0\,\mathrm{m}.\]

Final Answer:
The height of the water column is \(10.0\,\mathrm{m}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_FLUIDS_NUMERICAL_Q06 - Volume flow rate in pipe of uniform cross section

questiontext.text: An incompressible fluid flows through a pipe of uniform cross-sectional area \(4.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}^2\) at a constant speed of \(2.5\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\). What is the volume flux (flow rate) of the fluid?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Cross-sectional area: \(A = 4.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}^2\). Flow speed: \(v = 2.5\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formula
The volume flux or flow rate is given by the product of area and velocity: \[Q = A v.\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the values: \[Q = (4.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}^2) \times (2.5\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}) = 10.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}^3\,\mathrm{s}^{-1} = 1.0 \times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m}^3\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}.\]

Final Answer:
The volume flux of the fluid is \(1.0 \times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m}^3\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_FLUIDS_NUMERICAL_Q07 - Surface tension force on floating needle on water

questiontext.text: A thin straight wire of length \(5.0\,\mathrm{cm}\) floats horizontally on the surface of water. Taking the surface tension of water as \(0.073\,\mathrm{N}\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}\), what is the extra downward pull exerted by surface tension on the wire?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Length of wire: \(l = 5.0\,\mathrm{cm} = 0.050\,\mathrm{m}\). Surface tension of water: \(S = 0.073\,\mathrm{N}\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Relevant Principle
A wire resting on a liquid surface has two contact lines along its length (one on each side). Therefore, the total downward force exerted by surface tension is: \[F = 2 S l.\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the given quantities: \[F = 2 \times (0.073\,\mathrm{N}\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}) \times (0.050\,\mathrm{m}) = 0.146 \times 0.050 = 0.0073\,\mathrm{N} = 7.3 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{N}.\]

Final Answer:
The extra downward force exerted by surface tension is \(7.3 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{N}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_FLUIDS_NUMERICAL_Q08 - Average pressure sustained by human thigh bones

questiontext.text: The two thigh bones (femurs), each of cross-sectional area \(10\,\mathrm{cm}^2\), support the upper part of a human body of mass \(40\,\mathrm{kg}\). Taking \(g = 10\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}\), calculate the average pressure sustained by the femurs.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass supported: \(m = 40\,\mathrm{kg}\). Area of each femur: \(A_1 = 10\,\mathrm{cm}^2 = 10 \times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m}^2\). Total area: \(A = 2 \times 10 \times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m}^2 = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}^2\). Acceleration due to gravity: \(g = 10\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formula
Force acting vertically down: \(F = m g\). Average pressure: \[P_{\mathrm{av}} = \frac{F}{A} = \frac{m g}{A}.\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate force: \[F = 40\,\mathrm{kg} \times 10\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2} = 400\,\mathrm{N}.\] Calculate pressure: \[P_{\mathrm{av}} = \frac{400\,\mathrm{N}}{2.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}^2} = 2.0 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{N}\,\mathrm{m}^{-2}.\]

Final Answer:
The average pressure sustained by the femurs is \(2.0 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{N}\,\mathrm{m}^{-2}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_FLUIDS_NUMERICAL_Q09 - Absolute pressure on swimmer at ten metre depth

questiontext.text: A swimmer dives to a depth of \(10\,\mathrm{m}\) below the surface of a freshwater lake. Taking atmospheric pressure as \(1.01 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}\), density of water as \(1000\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\), and \(g = 10\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}\), what is the absolute pressure on the swimmer?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Depth: \(h = 10\,\mathrm{m}\). Density of water: \(\rho = 1000\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\). Atmospheric pressure: \(P_a = 1.01 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}\). Gravitational acceleration: \(g = 10\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formula
Absolute pressure at depth \(h\): \[P = P_a + \rho g h.\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Compute gauge pressure: \[\rho g h = 1000\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3} \times 10\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2} \times 10\,\mathrm{m} = 1.00 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}.\] Add atmospheric pressure: \[P = 1.01 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{Pa} + 1.00 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{Pa} = 2.01 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}.\]

Final Answer:
The absolute pressure on the swimmer is \(2.01 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_FLUIDS_NUMERICAL_Q10 - Atmosphere extension height assuming constant density

questiontext.text: The density of the atmosphere at sea level is \(1.29\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\). Assuming this density does not change with altitude, how high would the atmosphere extend? Take standard sea-level atmospheric pressure as \(1.01 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}\) and \(g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Atmospheric pressure: \(P_a = 1.01 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}\). Density: \(\rho = 1.29\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\). Gravitational acceleration: \(g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}\).

Step 2: Relevant Principle
The sea-level atmospheric pressure is supported by the weight of the air column: \[P_a = \rho g h \implies h = \frac{P_a}{\rho g}.\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate height: \[h = \frac{1.01 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}}{(1.29\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3})(9.8\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2})} = \frac{101000}{12.642} \approx 7989\,\mathrm{m} \approx 8\,\mathrm{km}.\]

Final Answer:
The atmosphere would extend to a height of \(7989\,\mathrm{m}\) (approximately \(8\,\mathrm{km}\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_FLUIDS_NUMERICAL_Q11 - Force on larger piston in connected hydraulic syringes

questiontext.text: Two syringes of different cross-sections filled with water are connected by a tightly fitted rubber tube. The diameters of the smaller and larger pistons are \(1.0\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(3.0\,\mathrm{cm}\) respectively. What force is exerted on the larger piston when a force of \(10\,\mathrm{N}\) is applied to the smaller piston?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Diameter of smaller piston: \(D_1 = 1.0\,\mathrm{cm}\). Diameter of larger piston: \(D_2 = 3.0\,\mathrm{cm}\). Force on smaller piston: \(F_1 = 10\,\mathrm{N}\).

Step 2: Relevant Principle
According to Pascal's law, pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted undiminished: \[P = \frac{F_1}{A_1} = \frac{F_2}{A_2} \implies F_2 = F_1 \left(\frac{A_2}{A_1}\right) = F_1 \left(\frac{D_2}{D_1}\right)^2.\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the values: \[F_2 = 10\,\mathrm{N} \times \left(\frac{3.0\,\mathrm{cm}}{1.0\,\mathrm{cm}}\right)^2 = 10 \times 9 = 90\,\mathrm{N}.\]

Final Answer:
The force exerted on the larger piston is \(90\,\mathrm{N}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_FLUIDS_NUMERICAL_Q12 - Outward displacement of larger piston in connected syringes

questiontext.text: In two connected water-filled syringes with piston diameters of \(1.0\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(3.0\,\mathrm{cm}\), the smaller piston is pushed inward through a distance of \(6.0\,\mathrm{cm}\). Assuming water is completely incompressible, how much does the larger piston move outward?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Displacement of smaller piston: \(L_1 = 6.0\,\mathrm{cm}\). Diameters: \(D_1 = 1.0\,\mathrm{cm}\), \(D_2 = 3.0\,\mathrm{cm}\).

Step 2: Relevant Principle
For an incompressible liquid, volume displaced inward by the smaller piston equals volume displaced outward by the larger piston: \[A_1 L_1 = A_2 L_2 \implies L_2 = L_1 \left(\frac{A_1}{A_2}\right) = L_1 \left(\frac{D_1}{D_2}\right)^2.\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Compute displacement: \[L_2 = 6.0\,\mathrm{cm} \times \left(\frac{1.0}{3.0}\right)^2 = \frac{6.0}{9} \approx 0.67\,\mathrm{cm}.\]

Final Answer:
The larger piston moves outward through \(0.67\,\mathrm{cm}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_FLUIDS_NUMERICAL_Q13 - Air pressure required in hydraulic car lift

questiontext.text: In a car lift, compressed air exerts a force on a small piston of radius \(5.0\,\mathrm{cm}\). This pressure is transmitted through a fluid to a second piston of radius \(15\,\mathrm{cm}\) that lifts a car of mass \(1350\,\mathrm{kg}\). Taking \(g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}\), what air pressure is necessary to accomplish this task?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Radius of larger piston: \(r_2 = 15\,\mathrm{cm} = 0.15\,\mathrm{m}\). Radius of smaller piston: \(r_1 = 5.0\,\mathrm{cm} = 0.050\,\mathrm{m}\). Mass of car: \(m = 1350\,\mathrm{kg}\). Gravitational acceleration: \(g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formula
The force needed to lift the car is \(F_2 = m g\). By Pascal's law, the pressure is transmitted undiminished: \[P = \frac{F_2}{A_2} = \frac{m g}{\pi r_2^2}.\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Compute the load and pressure: \[F_2 = 1350\,\mathrm{kg} \times 9.8\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2} = 13230\,\mathrm{N}.\] \[P = \frac{13230\,\mathrm{N}}{\pi (0.15\,\mathrm{m})^2} = \frac{13230}{3.1416 \times 0.0225} = \frac{13230}{0.070686} \approx 1.87 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{Pa} \approx 1.9 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}.\]

Final Answer:
The air pressure necessary is \(1.9 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_FLUIDS_NUMERICAL_Q14 - Pressure exerted by high heel on floor

questiontext.text: A \(50\,\mathrm{kg}\) person balances on a single circular high heel of diameter \(1.0\,\mathrm{cm}\). Taking \(g = 10\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}\), what is the pressure exerted by the heel on the horizontal floor?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass: \(m = 50\,\mathrm{kg}\). Diameter of heel: \(d = 1.0\,\mathrm{cm} = 1.0 \times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m}\). Radius: \(r = 0.50 \times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m}\). Acceleration due to gravity: \(g = 10\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formula
Force exerted: \(F = m g\). Area of circular heel: \(A = \pi r^2\). Pressure: \[P = \frac{F}{A} = \frac{m g}{\pi r^2}.\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate force: \[F = 50 \times 10 = 500\,\mathrm{N}.\] Calculate area: \[A = \pi (5.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m})^2 = 3.1416 \times 2.5 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m}^2 \approx 7.854 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m}^2.\] Calculate pressure: \[P = \frac{500}{7.854 \times 10^{-5}} \approx 6.366 \times 10^6\,\mathrm{Pa} \approx 6.4 \times 10^6\,\mathrm{Pa}.\]

Final Answer:
The pressure exerted by the heel on the floor is \(6.4 \times 10^6\,\mathrm{Pa}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_FLUIDS_NUMERICAL_Q15 - Height of French wine column in barometer

questiontext.text: Torricelli's barometer used mercury. Blaise Pascal duplicated the experiment using French wine of density \(984\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\). Determine the height of the wine column for a standard atmospheric pressure of \(1.013 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}\), taking \(g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}\).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Atmospheric pressure: \(P_a = 1.013 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}\). Density of wine: \(\rho = 984\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\). Acceleration due to gravity: \(g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}\).

Step 2: Relevant Principle
In a barometer, atmospheric pressure balances the hydrostatic pressure of the liquid column: \[P_a = \rho g h \implies h = \frac{P_a}{\rho g}.\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the parameters: \[h = \frac{1.013 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}}{(984\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3})(9.8\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2})} = \frac{101300}{9643.2} \approx 10.505\,\mathrm{m} \approx 10.5\,\mathrm{m}.\]

Final Answer:
The height of the wine column is \(10.5\,\mathrm{m}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_FLUIDS_NUMERICAL_Q16 - Viscosity calculation from sliding horizontal plate

questiontext.text: A metal plate of area \(0.10\,\mathrm{m}^2\) rests on a liquid film of thickness \(0.30\,\mathrm{mm}\) on a table. It is connected via a light string over an ideal pulley to a suspended mass of \(0.010\,\mathrm{kg}\). When released, the plate moves with a constant speed of \(0.085\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\). Taking \(g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}\), what is the coefficient of viscosity of the liquid?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Plate area: \(A = 0.10\,\mathrm{m}^2\). Film thickness: \(l = 0.30\,\mathrm{mm} = 0.30 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}\). Suspended mass: \(m = 0.010\,\mathrm{kg}\). Speed: \(v = 0.085\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\). Gravitational acceleration: \(g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formula
At constant speed, the viscous shear force equals the string tension: \(F = m g\). Viscosity formula: \[\eta = \frac{F / A}{v / l} = \frac{F l}{v A}.\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate force: \[F = 0.010 \times 9.8 = 0.098\,\mathrm{N}.\] Calculate viscosity: \[\eta = \frac{(0.098\,\mathrm{N})(0.30 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m})}{(0.085\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1})(0.10\,\mathrm{m}^2)} = \frac{2.94 \times 10^{-5}}{8.5 \times 10^{-3}} \approx 3.459 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{Pa}\,\mathrm{s} \approx 3.46 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{Pa}\,\mathrm{s}.\]

Final Answer:
The coefficient of viscosity of the liquid is \(3.46 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{Pa}\,\mathrm{s}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_FLUIDS_NUMERICAL_Q17 - Specific gravity of methylated spirit in manometer

questiontext.text: A U-tube contains water and methylated spirit separated by mercury in equilibrium. The mercury surfaces in the two arms are at the same horizontal level when the column of water is \(10.0\,\mathrm{cm}\) and the column of spirit is \(12.5\,\mathrm{cm}\). What is the specific gravity of the spirit?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Height of water column: \(h_w = 10.0\,\mathrm{cm}\). Height of spirit column: \(h_s = 12.5\,\mathrm{cm}\). Mercury levels are identical in both arms.

Step 2: Relevant Principle
At the level of the mercury interfaces, pressures exerted by the two liquid columns are equal: \[P_a + \rho_w g h_w = P_a + \rho_s g h_s \implies \rho_w h_w = \rho_s h_s.\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate specific gravity: \[\text{Specific gravity} = \frac{\rho_s}{\rho_w} = \frac{h_w}{h_s} = \frac{10.0\,\mathrm{cm}}{12.5\,\mathrm{cm}} = 0.80.\]

Final Answer:
The specific gravity of the spirit is \(0.80\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_FLUIDS_NUMERICAL_Q18 - Ejection speed of liquid through holes of spray pump

questiontext.text: The cylindrical tube of a spray pump has a cross-section of \(8.0\,\mathrm{cm}^2\), and one end has \(40\) fine holes each of diameter \(1.0\,\mathrm{mm}\). If the liquid flow speed inside the tube is \(1.5\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{min}^{-1}\), what is the speed of ejection of the liquid through the holes?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Tube cross-section: \(A_1 = 8.0\,\mathrm{cm}^2 = 8.0 \times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m}^2\). Flow speed in tube: \(v_1 = 1.5\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{min}^{-1} = \frac{1.5}{60}\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1} = 0.025\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\). Number of holes: \(n = 40\). Diameter of hole: \(d = 1.0\,\mathrm{mm} = 1.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}\). Radius of hole: \(r = 0.50 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}\).

Step 2: Relevant Principle
Equation of continuity for incompressible flow: \[A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2 = n (\pi r^2) v_2.\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Total area of \(40\) holes: \[A_2 = 40 \times \pi (0.50 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m})^2 = 40 \times 3.1416 \times 2.5 \times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{m}^2 = 3.1416 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m}^2.\] Compute ejection speed: \[v_2 = \frac{A_1 v_1}{A_2} = \frac{8.0 \times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m}^2 \times 0.025\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}}{3.1416 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m}^2} = \frac{2.0 \times 10^{-5}}{3.1416 \times 10^{-5}} \approx 0.6366\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1} \approx 0.64\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}.\]

Final Answer:
The speed of ejection through the holes is \(0.64\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_FLUIDS_NUMERICAL_Q19 - Surface tension of film supporting slider weight

questiontext.text: A U-shaped wire is dipped in a soap solution and removed, forming a thin soap film bounded by a light slider. The film supports a total weight of \(1.5 \times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{N}\) (including the slider). If the length of the slider is \(30\,\mathrm{cm}\), what is the surface tension of the film?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Weight supported: \(W = 1.5 \times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{N}\). Length of slider: \(l = 30\,\mathrm{cm} = 0.30\,\mathrm{m}\).

Step 2: Relevant Principle
A liquid film in air has two free surfaces. Hence, the upward surface tension force is: \[F = 2 S l.\] In equilibrium: \[2 S l = W \implies S = \frac{W}{2 l}.\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the values: \[S = \frac{1.5 \times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{N}}{2 \times 0.30\,\mathrm{m}} = \frac{1.5 \times 10^{-2}}{0.60} = 2.5 \times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{N}\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}.\]

Final Answer:
The surface tension of the film is \(2.5 \times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{N}\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_FLUIDS_NUMERICAL_Q20 - Excess pressure inside spherical mercury drop

questiontext.text: What is the excess pressure inside a spherical drop of mercury of radius \(3.00\,\mathrm{mm}\) at \(20^\circ\mathrm{C}\), given that the surface tension of mercury at \(20^\circ\mathrm{C}\) is \(4.65 \times 10^{-1}\,\mathrm{N}\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Radius of drop: \(r = 3.00\,\mathrm{mm} = 3.00 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}\). Surface tension: \(S = 4.65 \times 10^{-1}\,\mathrm{N}\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Relevant Principle
A liquid drop has only one liquid-gas interface. The excess pressure inside is given by: \[\Delta P = \frac{2 S}{r}.\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate excess pressure: \[\Delta P = \frac{2 \times 4.65 \times 10^{-1}\,\mathrm{N}\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}}{3.00 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}} = \frac{0.93}{3.00 \times 10^{-3}} = 310\,\mathrm{Pa}.\]

Final Answer:
The excess pressure inside the mercury drop is \(310\,\mathrm{Pa}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_FLUIDS_NUMERICAL_Q21 - Speed of efflux from open tank orifice

questiontext.text: A large open reservoir contains water with a free surface open to the atmosphere. A small hole is drilled into its side wall at a vertical depth of \(4.9\,\mathrm{m}\) below the water level. Taking \(g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}\), what is the speed of efflux of water leaving the hole?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Depth of hole: \(h = 4.9\,\mathrm{m}\). Gravitational acceleration: \(g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}\).

Step 2: Relevant Principle
By Torricelli's law, the speed of efflux from an open tank under gravity is identical to the speed of free fall from depth \(h\): \[v = \sqrt{2 g h}.\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate the velocity: \[v = \sqrt{2 \times 9.8\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2} \times 4.9\,\mathrm{m}} = \sqrt{96.04} = 9.8\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}.\]

Final Answer:
The speed of efflux is \(9.8\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_FLUIDS_NUMERICAL_Q22 - Wing pressure difference supporting aircraft in level flight

questiontext.text: A Boeing aircraft of mass \(3.3 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{kg}\) has a total wing area of \(500\,\mathrm{m}^2\). In level horizontal flight, taking \(g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}\), what is the estimated pressure difference between the lower and upper surfaces of the wings?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of aircraft: \(M = 3.3 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{kg}\). Total wing area: \(A = 500\,\mathrm{m}^2\). Acceleration due to gravity: \(g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}\).

Step 2: Relevant Principle
In level flight, the upward aerodynamic force from the pressure difference balances the weight: \[\Delta P \cdot A = M g \implies \Delta P = \frac{M g}{A}.\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Compute pressure difference: \[\Delta P = \frac{3.3 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{kg} \times 9.8\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}}{500\,\mathrm{m}^2} = \frac{3.234 \times 10^6}{500} = 6468\,\mathrm{N}\,\mathrm{m}^{-2} \approx 6.5 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{N}\,\mathrm{m}^{-2}.\]

Final Answer:
The pressure difference between the wing surfaces is \(6.5 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{N}\,\mathrm{m}^{-2}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_FLUIDS_NUMERICAL_Q23 - Ratio of terminal velocities of two spheres

questiontext.text: Two solid spheres made of the same material have radii in the ratio \(1 : 3\). When dropped into a tall column of viscous liquid, what is the ratio of their terminal velocities?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Ratio of radii: \(\frac{a_1}{a_2} = \frac{1}{3}\). Both spheres have identical density and fall in the same viscous fluid.

Step 2: Relevant Principle
From Stokes' law, terminal velocity is given by: \[v_t = \frac{2 a^2 (\rho - \sigma) g}{9 \eta}.\] For constant densities and viscosity, \(v_t \propto a^2\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Evaluate the ratio: \[\frac{v_{t1}}{v_{t2}} = \left(\frac{a_1}{a_2}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{9}.\]

Final Answer:
The ratio of their terminal velocities is \(1 : 9\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_FLUIDS_NUMERICAL_Q24 - Excess pressure inside spherical soap bubble

questiontext.text: What is the excess pressure inside a spherical soap bubble of radius \(5.0\,\mathrm{mm}\) formed in air, given that the surface tension of the soap solution is \(2.50 \times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{N}\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Radius of soap bubble: \(r = 5.0\,\mathrm{mm} = 5.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}\). Surface tension: \(S = 2.50 \times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{N}\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Relevant Principle
A soap bubble in air has two liquid-air interfaces (inner and outer). Thus, the excess pressure inside the bubble is: \[\Delta P = \frac{4 S}{r}.\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate excess pressure: \[\Delta P = \frac{4 \times 2.50 \times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{N}\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}}{5.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}} = \frac{0.100}{0.0050} = 20\,\mathrm{Pa}.\]

Final Answer:
The excess pressure inside the soap bubble is \(20\,\mathrm{Pa}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_FLUIDS_NUMERICAL_Q25 - Work done in stretching a rectangular liquid film

questiontext.text: A rectangular liquid film has a movable horizontal wire slider of length \(10\,\mathrm{cm}\). If the slider is moved by a distance of \(2.0\,\mathrm{cm}\) parallel to itself to stretch the film, what is the work done against surface tension? (Take the surface tension of the liquid as \(0.040\,\mathrm{N}\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Length of slider: \(l = 10\,\mathrm{cm} = 0.10\,\mathrm{m}\). Displacement of slider: \(d = 2.0\,\mathrm{cm} = 0.020\,\mathrm{m}\). Surface tension: \(S = 0.040\,\mathrm{N}\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Relevant Principle
A liquid film in air has two free surfaces. The increase in total surface area is: \[\Delta A = 2 \times (l \times d) = 2 l d.\] The work done against surface tension is: \[W = S \Delta A = 2 S l d.\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate work: \[W = 2 \times (0.040\,\mathrm{N}\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}) \times (0.10\,\mathrm{m}) \times (0.020\,\mathrm{m}) = 0.080 \times 0.0020 = 1.6 \times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{J}.\]

Final Answer:
The work done in stretching the film is \(1.6 \times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{J}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_FLUIDS_NUMERICAL_Q26 - Net compressive force on submarine window at ocean depth

questiontext.text: A submarine cruises at a depth of \(1000\,\mathrm{m}\) in sea water of density \(1.03 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\). The submarine has a square window of area \(20\,\mathrm{cm} \times 20\,\mathrm{cm}\), and its interior is maintained at sea-level atmospheric pressure. Taking \(g = 10\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}\), what is the net compressive force acting inward on the window?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Depth: \(h = 1000\,\mathrm{m}\). Sea water density: \(\rho = 1.03 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\). Gravitational acceleration: \(g = 10\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}\). Area of window: \(A = 0.20\,\mathrm{m} \times 0.20\,\mathrm{m} = 0.040\,\mathrm{m}^2\). Interior pressure: \(P_{\mathrm{in}} = P_a\).

Step 2: Relevant Principle
The external pressure is \(P_{\mathrm{out}} = P_a + \rho g h\). The net inward pressure is the gauge pressure: \[P_{\mathrm{net}} = P_{\mathrm{out}} - P_{\mathrm{in}} = \rho g h.\] The net inward force is: \[F = P_{\mathrm{net}} A = \rho g h A.\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate gauge pressure: \[P_{\mathrm{net}} = 1.03 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3} \times 10\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2} \times 1000\,\mathrm{m} = 1.03 \times 10^7\,\mathrm{Pa}.\] Compute force on window: \[F = 1.03 \times 10^7\,\mathrm{Pa} \times 0.040\,\mathrm{m}^2 = 4.12 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{N}.\]

Final Answer:
The net inward force acting on the window is \(4.12 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{N}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_FLUIDS_NUMERICAL_Q27 - Absolute hydrostatic pressure at three kilometre ocean depth

questiontext.text: A vertical offshore structure is built to withstand a maximum stress of \(10^9\,\mathrm{Pa}\). What is the total absolute hydrostatic pressure at the ocean floor at a depth of \(3.0\,\mathrm{km}\)? (Take sea water density as \(1.03 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\), atmospheric pressure as \(1.01 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}\), and \(g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Depth: \(h = 3.0\,\mathrm{km} = 3000\,\mathrm{m}\). Density: \(\rho = 1.03 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\). Gravitational acceleration: \(g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}\). Atmospheric pressure: \(P_a = 1.01 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formula
Absolute pressure at depth \(h\): \[P = P_a + \rho g h.\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Compute the gauge pressure: \[\rho g h = 1.03 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3} \times 9.8\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2} \times 3000\,\mathrm{m} = 3.0282 \times 10^7\,\mathrm{Pa}.\] Add atmospheric pressure: \[P = 1.01 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{Pa} + 3.0282 \times 10^7\,\mathrm{Pa} = 0.0101 \times 10^7\,\mathrm{Pa} + 3.0282 \times 10^7\,\mathrm{Pa} = 3.0383 \times 10^7\,\mathrm{Pa} \approx 3.04 \times 10^7\,\mathrm{Pa}.\]

Final Answer:
The absolute hydrostatic pressure is \(3.04 \times 10^7\,\mathrm{Pa}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_FLUIDS_NUMERICAL_Q28 - Mercury level difference upon pouring additional liquids in manometer

questiontext.text: A U-tube contains mercury in level, balanced initially by \(10.0\,\mathrm{cm}\) of water in one arm and \(12.5\,\mathrm{cm}\) of spirit (specific gravity \(0.80\)) in the other. If \(15.0\,\mathrm{cm}\) of water and \(15.0\,\mathrm{cm}\) of spirit are further poured into their respective arms, what is the resulting difference in the levels of mercury in the two arms? (Specific gravity of mercury is \(13.6\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Total height of water: \(h_w = 10.0 + 15.0 = 25.0\,\mathrm{cm}\). Total height of spirit: \(h_s = 12.5 + 15.0 = 27.5\,\mathrm{cm}\). Specific gravities: \(s_w = 1.0\), \(s_s = 0.80\), \(s_m = 13.6\).

Step 2: Relevant Principle
Equating pressures at the lower mercury meniscus: \[h_w \rho_w g = h_s \rho_s g + h \rho_m g \implies h_w = h_s (s_s) + h (s_m).\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the values: \[25.0 = 27.5 \times 0.80 + 13.6 \cdot h.\] \[27.5 \times 0.80 = 22.0\,\mathrm{cm} \implies 25.0 - 22.0 = 13.6 \cdot h \implies 3.0 = 13.6 \cdot h.\] \[h = \frac{3.0}{13.6} \approx 0.2206\,\mathrm{cm} \approx 0.221\,\mathrm{cm}.\]

Final Answer:
The difference in mercury levels in the two arms is \(0.221\,\mathrm{cm}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_FLUIDS_NUMERICAL_Q29 - Pressure difference for steady viscous flow through tube

questiontext.text: Glycerine of density \(1.3 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\) and viscosity \(0.83\,\mathrm{Pa}\,\mathrm{s}\) flows steadily through a horizontal tube of length \(1.5\,\mathrm{m}\) and radius \(1.0\,\mathrm{cm}\). If the mass of glycerine collected per second is \(4.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\), what is the pressure difference between the two ends of the tube? (Use Poiseuille's formula: \(Q = \frac{\pi \Delta P r^4}{8 \eta L}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Length: \(L = 1.5\,\mathrm{m}\). Radius: \(r = 1.0\,\mathrm{cm} = 1.0 \times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m}\). Density: \(\rho = 1.3 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\). Viscosity: \(\eta = 0.83\,\mathrm{Pa}\,\mathrm{s}\). Mass flow rate: \(\frac{d m}{d t} = 4.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Volume Flow Rate
The volume flow rate \(Q\) is: \[Q = \frac{1}{\rho}\frac{d m}{d t} = \frac{4.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}}{1.3 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}} \approx 3.077 \times 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m}^3\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}.\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Rearrange Poiseuille's equation: \[\Delta P = \frac{8 \eta L Q}{\pi r^4}.\] Substitute parameters with \(r^4 = 1.0 \times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{m}^4\): \[\Delta P = \frac{8 \times 0.83 \times 1.5 \times 3.077 \times 10^{-6}}{\pi \times 1.0 \times 10^{-8}} = \frac{9.96 \times 3.077 \times 10^{-6}}{3.1416 \times 10^{-8}} \approx 975.5\,\mathrm{Pa} \approx 9.8 \times 10^2\,\mathrm{Pa}.\]

Final Answer:
The pressure difference between the ends of the tube is \(9.8 \times 10^2\,\mathrm{Pa}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_FLUIDS_NUMERICAL_Q30 - Dynamic lift on model aeroplane wing in wind tunnel

questiontext.text: In a wind-tunnel test on a model aeroplane, air flow speeds over the upper and lower surfaces of the wing are \(70\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\) and \(63\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\) respectively. If the total wing area is \(2.5\,\mathrm{m}^2\) and the density of air is \(1.3\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\), what is the dynamic lift generated on the wing?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Upper speed: \(v_2 = 70\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\). Lower speed: \(v_1 = 63\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\). Wing area: \(A = 2.5\,\mathrm{m}^2\). Air density: \(\rho = 1.3\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\).

Step 2: Relevant Principle
By Bernoulli's principle across horizontal streamlines: \[\Delta P = \frac{1}{2}\rho (v_2^2 - v_1^2).\] The aerodynamic lift force is: \[F_{\text{lift}} = \Delta P \cdot A = \frac{1}{2}\rho (v_2^2 - v_1^2) A.\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate velocity square difference: \[v_2^2 - v_1^2 = 70^2 - 63^2 = 4900 - 3969 = 931\,\mathrm{m}^2\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}.\] Compute pressure difference: \[\Delta P = \frac{1}{2} \times 1.3\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3} \times 931\,\mathrm{m}^2\,\mathrm{s}^{-2} = 605.15\,\mathrm{N}\,\mathrm{m}^{-2}.\] Compute lift: \[F_{\text{lift}} = 605.15\,\mathrm{N}\,\mathrm{m}^{-2} \times 2.5\,\mathrm{m}^2 = 1512.875\,\mathrm{N} \approx 1.51 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{N}.\]

Final Answer:
The dynamic lift on the wing is \(1.51 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{N}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_FLUIDS_NUMERICAL_Q31 - Total pressure inside air bubble formed at depth in soap solution

questiontext.text: An air bubble of radius \(5.0\,\mathrm{mm}\) is formed at a depth of \(40.0\,\mathrm{cm}\) inside a vessel filled with soap solution of relative density \(1.20\). The surface tension of the soap solution is \(2.50 \times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{N}\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}\), atmospheric pressure is \(1.01 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}\), and \(g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}\). What is the total absolute pressure inside the bubble?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Radius of bubble: \(r = 5.0\,\mathrm{mm} = 5.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}\). Depth: \(h = 40.0\,\mathrm{cm} = 0.40\,\mathrm{m}\). Solution density: \(\rho = 1.20 \times 1000 = 1200\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\). Surface tension: \(S = 2.50 \times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{N}\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}\). Atmospheric pressure: \(P_a = 1.01 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}\). Gravitational acceleration: \(g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}\).

Step 2: Relevant Principles
An air bubble submerged in liquid has only one liquid-gas interface. The excess pressure inside is: \[\Delta P = \frac{2 S}{r}.\] The total pressure inside is: \[P_i = P_a + \rho g h + \frac{2 S}{r}.\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate hydrostatic pressure: \[\rho g h = 1200 \times 9.8 \times 0.40 = 4704\,\mathrm{Pa}.\] Calculate excess pressure: \[\Delta P = \frac{2 \times 2.50 \times 10^{-2}}{5.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 10\,\mathrm{Pa}.\] Calculate total pressure: \[P_i = 101000\,\mathrm{Pa} + 4704\,\mathrm{Pa} + 10\,\mathrm{Pa} = 105714\,\mathrm{Pa} \approx 1.057 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}.\]

Final Answer:
The total pressure inside the bubble is \(1.057 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_FLUIDS_NUMERICAL_Q32 - Fractional increase in airflow speed over aircraft wing

questiontext.text: A Boeing aircraft flies horizontally at an average speed of \(960\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{h}^{-1}\). The pressure difference required across its wings to sustain level flight is \(\Delta P = 6.5 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{N}\,\mathrm{m}^{-2}\). Taking the density of air as \(\rho = 1.2\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\), what is the fractional increase in the speed of air over the upper surface relative to the average speed, \(\frac{v_2 - v_1}{v_{\mathrm{av}}}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Pressure difference: \(\Delta P = 6.5 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{N}\,\mathrm{m}^{-2}\). Air density: \(\rho = 1.2\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\). Flight speed: \(v_{\mathrm{av}} = 960\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{h}^{-1} = \frac{960 \times 1000}{3600}\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1} = 267\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formula
From Bernoulli's equation: \[\Delta P = \frac{1}{2}\rho (v_2^2 - v_1^2) = \rho (v_2 - v_1) v_{\mathrm{av}} \implies \frac{v_2 - v_1}{v_{\mathrm{av}}} = \frac{\Delta P}{\rho v_{\mathrm{av}}^2}.\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate the ratio: \[\frac{v_2 - v_1}{v_{\mathrm{av}}} = \frac{6.5 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{N}\,\mathrm{m}^{-2}}{(1.2\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3})(267\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1})^2} = \frac{6500}{1.2 \times 71289} = \frac{6500}{85546.8} \approx 0.076 \approx 0.08.\]

Final Answer:
The fractional increase in speed is approximately \(0.08\) (or \(8\%\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_FLUIDS_NUMERICAL_Q33 - Oil viscosity from falling copper sphere terminal velocity

questiontext.text: A copper ball of radius \(2.0\,\mathrm{mm}\) falls at a terminal velocity of \(6.5\,\mathrm{cm}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\) through a tank of oil at \(20^\circ\mathrm{C}\). Density of oil is \(1.5 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\), density of copper is \(8.9 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\), and \(g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}\). What is the coefficient of viscosity of the oil?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Radius of sphere: \(a = 2.0\,\mathrm{mm} = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}\). Terminal velocity: \(v_t = 6.5\,\mathrm{cm}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1} = 6.5 \times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\). Density of copper: \(\rho = 8.9 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\). Density of oil: \(\sigma = 1.5 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\). Gravitational acceleration: \(g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formula
From Stokes' law: \[v_t = \frac{2 a^2 (\rho - \sigma) g}{9 \eta} \implies \eta = \frac{2 a^2 (\rho - \sigma) g}{9 v_t}.\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate density difference: \(\rho - \sigma = 7.4 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\). Substitute values: \[\eta = \frac{2 \times (2.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m})^2 \times (7.4 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}) \times (9.8\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2})}{9 \times (6.5 \times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1})} = \frac{2 \times 4.0 \times 10^{-6} \times 72520}{0.585} = \frac{0.58016}{0.585} \approx 0.9917\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1} \approx 0.99\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}.\]

Final Answer:
The coefficient of viscosity of the oil is \(0.99\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_FLUIDS_NUMERICAL_Q34 - Capillary rise of water in narrow glass tube

questiontext.text: A clean glass capillary tube of internal radius \(0.25\,\mathrm{mm}\) is inserted vertically into water. Given that the surface tension of water is \(7.3 \times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{N}\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}\), contact angle is \(0^\circ\), density of water is \(1000\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\), and \(g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}\), what is the height of capillary rise?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Tube radius: \(a = 0.25\,\mathrm{mm} = 2.5 \times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m}\). Surface tension: \(S = 7.3 \times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{N}\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}\). Contact angle: \(\theta = 0^\circ\) (\(\cos 0^\circ = 1\)). Density: \(\rho = 1000\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}\). Gravitational acceleration: \(g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formula
The capillary rise formula is: \[h = \frac{2 S \cos\theta}{\rho g a}.\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate height: \[h = \frac{2 \times (7.3 \times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{N}\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}) \times 1}{(1000\,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3})(9.8\,\mathrm{m}\,\mathrm{s}^{-2})(2.5 \times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m})} = \frac{0.146}{2.45} \approx 0.05959\,\mathrm{m} \approx 5.96\,\mathrm{cm}.\]

Final Answer:
The height of capillary rise is \(5.96\,\mathrm{cm}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_FLUIDS_NUMERICAL_Q35 - Work required to expand radius of soap bubble

questiontext.text: How much work must be done against surface tension to increase the radius of a spherical soap bubble in air from \(2.0\,\mathrm{cm}\) to \(4.0\,\mathrm{cm}\), if the surface tension of the soap solution is \(3.0 \times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{N}\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial radius: \(r_1 = 2.0\,\mathrm{cm} = 0.020\,\mathrm{m}\). Final radius: \(r_2 = 4.0\,\mathrm{cm} = 0.040\,\mathrm{m}\). Surface tension: \(S = 3.0 \times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{N}\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Relevant Principle
A soap bubble has two free surfaces. The total increase in surface area is: \[\Delta A = 2 \times (4\pi r_2^2 - 4\pi r_1^2) = 8\pi (r_2^2 - r_1^2).\] The work done is: \[W = S \Delta A = 8\pi S (r_2^2 - r_1^2).\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate area change factor: \[r_2^2 - r_1^2 = (0.040\,\mathrm{m})^2 - (0.020\,\mathrm{m})^2 = 0.0016 - 0.0004 = 0.0012\,\mathrm{m}^2 = 1.2 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}^2.\] Calculate work: \[W = 8 \times 3.1416 \times (3.0 \times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{N}\,\mathrm{m}^{-1}) \times (1.2 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}^2) = 25.1328 \times 3.6 \times 10^{-5} \approx 9.048 \times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{J} \approx 9.05 \times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{J}.\]

Final Answer:
The work required to expand the bubble is \(9.05 \times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{J}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MECHANICAL_PROPERTIES_OF_FLUIDS_NUMERICAL_Q36 - Curvature radius of common partition between touching bubbles

questiontext.text: Two soap bubbles of radii \(r_1 = 3.0\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(r_2 = 6.0\,\mathrm{cm}\) coalesce in air so that they have a common interface. What is the radius of curvature of this common interface?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Radius of first bubble: \(r_1 = 3.0\,\mathrm{cm}\). Radius of second bubble: \(r_2 = 6.0\,\mathrm{cm}\).

Step 2: Relevant Principle
The excess pressure in each bubble is \(\Delta P_1 = \frac{4 S}{r_1}\) and \(\Delta P_2 = \frac{4 S}{r_2}\). The pressure difference across the common interface of radius of curvature \(R\) is: \[P_1 - P_2 = \frac{4 S}{R} = 4 S \left(\frac{1}{r_1} - \frac{1}{r_2}\right) \implies \frac{1}{R} = \frac{1}{r_1} - \frac{1}{r_2} \implies R = \frac{r_1 r_2}{r_2 - r_1}.\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the radii: \[R = \frac{3.0\,\mathrm{cm} \times 6.0\,\mathrm{cm}}{6.0\,\mathrm{cm} - 3.0\,\mathrm{cm}} = \frac{18.0}{3.0} = 6.0\,\mathrm{cm}.\]

Final Answer:
The radius of curvature of the common interface is \(6.0\,\mathrm{cm}\).
